t.1.1.0: Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, and to Nara, the best of men, and to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then recite the Jaya.
t.1.1.2: Once the son of the Sūta, bowed down in humility, approached the brahmarṣis of rigorous vows as they sat together.
t.1.1.1: Ugraśravas, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a sūta and bard versed in the Purāṇas, at the twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, the master of the household, in the Naimiṣa forest…
t.1.1.4: With joined palms he saluted all those sages, and, welcomed in turn by the virtuous ones, he asked after the growth of their austerities.
t.1.1.3: When he had arrived at the hermitage, the ascetics who dwelt in the Naimiṣa forest gathered around him there, eager to hear his wondrous tales.
t.1.1.6: Then, noticing that he was comfortably seated and rested, one of the seers there questioned him, opening the way for stories.
t.1.1.5: Then, when all those ascetics had taken their seats, Lomaharṣaṇi, out of humility, took the seat that had been assigned to him.
t.1.1.7: Whence have you come, Sauti, and where have you spent this time, O lotus-petal-eyed one? Tell me this, for I am asking.
t.1.1.8: At the snake sacrifice of the great-souled royal seer Janamejaya, duly in the presence of that lord of kings, the son of Parikṣit,
t.1.1.9: The many and most holy tales proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, which were also duly recounted by Vaiśampāyana.
t.1.1.11: I went to the holy land called Samantapañcaka, frequented by the twice-born, that region where of old the battle took place between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus and all the kings of the earth.
t.1.1.10: Having heard those tales of wondrous meaning that rest upon the Mahābhārata, and having wandered through many sacred fords and sanctuaries, I…
t.1.1.12: Therefore, wishing to see you, I have come here into your presence; for all of you, long-lived ones, are regarded by me as having become one with Brahman.
t.1.1.13: At this sacrifice, O twice-born ones, you illustrious men, radiant as the sun and fire, have performed your ablutions, are pure, have completed your recitations and made your offerings into the fire, and now sit at ease; what shall I tell you?
t.1.1.14: Holy tales drawn from the Purāṇas, or tales grounded in dharma, and the history of kings and of great-souled seers.
t.1.1.15: That ancient lore which was proclaimed by Dvaipāyana, the supreme seer, and which the gods and the brahmin seers honored after hearing it.
t.1.1.16: Of that most excellent of narratives, with its varied words and sections, endowed with subtle meanings and sound reasoning, and adorned with the meanings of the Vedas—
t.1.1.17: the holy, Brahmic composition of the Bhārata history, endowed with the meaning of its text, refined and polished, and amplified by various treatises,
t.1.1.19: We wish to hear the saṃhitā of Vyāsa of wondrous deeds, which is equal to the four Vedas, righteous, and which takes away the fear of sin.
t.1.1.18: That tale which the seer Vaiśampāyana duly recounted with delight to King Janamejaya at the sacrificial session, at the command of Dvaipāyana.
t.1.1.22: Having bowed down to Viṣṇu, the auspicious and the bringer of auspiciousness, the most excellent, the sinless and pure, to Hṛṣīkeśa, Hari, the teacher of all that moves and does not move,
t.1.1.20: The primeval Person, the Lord, invoked by many and praised by many, the True, the one imperishable syllable, Brahman, both manifest and unmanifest, eternal—
t.1.1.21: Him who is both non-being and being, who is the universe that lies beyond being and non-being, the creator of the high and the low, the ancient, the supreme, the imperishable one.
t.1.1.23: Here I shall declare in full the thought of the great seer Vyāsa, the great-souled one of immeasurable splendour, who is honoured throughout all the world.
t.1.1.24: Some poets have told this history before, others are telling it now, and still others will tell it in the same way upon the earth.
t.1.1.25: But this great knowledge is established in the three worlds, which is preserved by the twice-born both in its detailed forms and in its condensed forms.
t.1.1.26: Adorned with auspicious words and with conventions both divine and human, and endowed with various metres, it is dear to the learned.
t.1.1.27: When all this was without radiance and without light, enveloped on every side by darkness, there came into being a single great egg, the imperishable seed of all creatures.
t.1.1.29: It is wondrous and inconceivable, everywhere attained to sameness; it is the unmanifest, subtle cause, that which is of the nature of both being and non-being.
t.1.1.28: At the beginning of the yuga, they declare that to be the great and divine cause, in which, it is heard, abides that truth, the light, the eternal brahman.
t.1.1.31: Likewise Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, and the seven sons of Dakṣa; then there came into being the twenty-one lords of creatures.
t.1.1.30: From it was born the Grandsire, the one lord Prajāpati: Brahmā, the teacher of the gods, Sthāṇu, Manu, Ka, and Parameṣṭhin.
t.1.1.32: And the Puruṣa of immeasurable self, whom the ṛṣis know as the All; likewise the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and also the two Aśvins.
t.1.1.34: And many royal sages endowed with all virtues; the waters, heaven, earth, wind, the atmosphere, and likewise the directions.
t.1.1.33: Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and likewise the Pitṛs; then were born the learned, cultivated, and spotless Brahmarṣis.
t.1.1.35: The year, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, days and nights came into being in due order, and whatever else there is that the world witnesses, all of that came into being.
t.1.1.36: Whatever being is seen here, whether stationary or moving, this whole world is drawn back together again when the end of the yuga has arrived.
t.1.1.38: Thus this wheel, without beginning or end, which brings about the destruction of beings, revolves in the world, having neither origin nor dissolution.
t.1.1.37: Just as, in each season, the various signs of the season appear in their turn, those very same ones again and again, so too do the states of things appear at the beginnings of the yugas.
t.1.1.39: Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred, and thirty-three: such, described in brief, is the creation of the gods.
t.1.1.40: Divasputra, Bṛhadbhānu, Cakṣus, Ātman, Vibhāvasu, Savitṛ, Ṛcīka, Arka, Bhānu, Āśāvaha and Ravi.
t.1.1.41: All these were the sons of Vivasvat, and Mahya was likewise the youngest of them. Devabhrāj was his son, and from him came the one remembered as Subhrāj.
t.1.1.42: From Subhrāj came three sons, rich in offspring and deeply learned: Daśajyoti, Śatajyoti, and the self-possessed Sahasrajyoti.
t.1.1.43: The great-souled Daśajyoti had ten thousand sons, and here Śatajyoti had other sons, ten times as many as those.
t.1.1.44: Then again, the sons of Sahasrajyotis were ten times as many; from them came this lineage of the Kurus, of the Yadus, and of Bharata.
t.1.1.45: The lineage of Yayāti and Ikṣvāku, and in every way the many dynasties of the royal seers that arose, and the creations of beings, all set forth in full detail.
t.1.1.46: All the abodes of beings, and that which is the threefold mystery, the Veda and Yoga together with their knowledge, dharma, artha, and kāma as well.
t.1.1.48: The histories together with their explanations, and the various sacred revelations as well: all this has been set forth in order here, and the defining character of the book has been declared.
t.1.1.49: Having set forth this great knowledge in full, the seer then spoke it in brief; for the learned in this world value holding it both in concise and in expanded form.
t.1.1.47: The ṛṣi beheld the treatises on dharma, kāma and artha, and treatises of many other kinds, and the ordering of the world's course that had come into being.
t.1.1.50: Some brahmins study the Bhārata thoroughly beginning from Manu, others likewise beginning from Āstīka, and still others beginning from Uparicara.
t.1.1.51: The wise illuminate the manifold knowledge of the Saṃhitā; some are skilled at expounding it, others at retaining the text in memory.
t.1.1.52: Through austerity and celibate discipline, the son of Satyavatī divided the eternal Veda and then composed this sacred history.
t.1.1.54: Long ago, in the field of Vicitravīrya, the mighty Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana begot three Kauravyas, like three fires.
t.1.1.55: Having begotten Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu, and Vidura as well, the wise one went back once more to his hermitage for the sake of austerity.
t.1.1.53: The son of Parāśara, the learned brahmarṣi of rigorous vows, righteous in spirit, at the behest of his mother and of the wise Gāṅgeya…
t.1.1.56: When they had been born, had grown old, and had gone to the supreme state, the great seer told the Bhārata in this world of men.
t.1.1.57: Being asked by Janamejaya and by brāhmaṇas in their thousands, he instructed his disciple Vaiśampāyana, who was seated near him.
t.1.1.58: Seated together with the members of the assembly, he recited the Bhārata in the intervals between the rites of the sacrifice, being urged on again and again.
t.1.1.59: Dvaipāyana fully described the expanse of the Kuru lineage, the righteous character of Gāndhārī, the wisdom of the Kṣattṛ, and the steadfastness of Kuntī.
t.1.1.60: The blessed seer has proclaimed the greatness of Vāsudeva, the truthfulness of the Pāṇḍavas, and the misconduct of the Dhārtarāṣṭras.
t.1.1.61: He composed the Bhārata collection of twenty-four thousand verses; without the subsidiary tales, just so much is called the Bhārata by the wise.
t.1.1.63: Dvaipāyana first taught this to his son Śuka; then the lord imparted it to other disciples who were worthy of it.
t.1.1.62: Then the seer further composed a summary of one hundred and fifty verses, the chapter called Anukramaṇī, setting out the events together with their parvans.
t.1.1.64: Nārada recited it to the gods, Asita Devala to the ancestors, and Śuka recited it to the Gandharvas, Yakṣas and Rākṣasas.
t.1.1.65: Duryodhana is a great tree made of wrath; Karṇa is its trunk, Śakuni its branches, Duḥśāsana its abundant flowers and fruit, and the root is the unwise king Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
t.1.1.67: Pāṇḍu, having conquered many lands by battle and by valor, then dwelt in the forest together with his people, devoted to hunting.
t.1.1.66: Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree made of dharma; Arjuna is its trunk, Bhīmasena its branches, and the two sons of Mādrī its abundant flowers and fruits. Its root is Kṛṣṇa, the Veda, and the brahmins.
t.1.1.68: In the slaying of the deer in the act of mating, he met with a grievous calamity; and there, from the birth of the Pārthas onward, came the due sequence of customary rites and observances.
t.1.1.70: Protected by their two mothers, they grew up together with the ascetics in pure and holy forests and in the hermitages of great men.
t.1.1.69: And the coming of Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and likewise of the two gods, the Aśvins, to the two mothers, in accordance with the secret teaching of dharma.
t.1.1.71: And then they were brought by the seers themselves to the Dhārtarāṣṭras: children, handsome, wearing matted locks, living as brahmacārins.
t.1.1.72: "These Pāṇḍavas are your sons, your brothers, your disciples and your friends": having said this, the sages then vanished.
t.1.1.73: Then, seeing those Pāṇḍavas presented by them, the Kauravas, the learned men, the classes, and those who were townsfolk all cried out loudly with joy.
t.1.1.74: Some said, "These are not his," while others said, "These are his"; and still others asked, "Since Pāṇḍu has long been dead, how can they be his?"
t.1.1.75: "Welcome in every way! By good fortune we behold the offspring of Pāṇḍu! Let 'welcome' be spoken!" Such words were heard on every side.
t.1.1.76: When that sound had ceased, all the directions resounded, and a tumultuous clamor of invisible beings arose.
t.1.1.77: At the entrance of the Pārthas there was an auspicious shower of flowers, fragrances, and the sounds of conches and kettledrums; it was like a marvel.
t.1.1.78: And out of affection for them, a great sound arose there from all the citizens, born of joy, touching the heavens and spreading their fame.
t.1.1.79: Having studied all the Vedas and the various treatises, the Pāṇḍavas too lived there, honored and fearing nothing from any quarter.
t.1.1.80: The subjects were pleased by the purity of Yudhiṣṭhira, by the steadfastness of Bhīmasena, and by the valor of Arjuna.
t.1.1.82: Then, at a gathering of kings, Arjuna, having performed a most difficult feat, won Kṛṣṇā, the maiden who was choosing her own husband.
t.1.1.83: From that time on he became, in this world, one to be honored by all bearers of the bow, and in battles too he was as hard to look upon as the sun.
t.1.1.81: The whole world was delighted by their dutiful obedience to Kuntī, their elder, by the modesty of the twins, and by their heroic excellence.
t.1.1.84: Having conquered all the kings and all the great hosts, that Arjuna brought to the king the Rājasūya, the great sacrifice.
t.1.1.85: Yudhiṣṭhira accomplished the Rājasūya, the great sacrifice, rich in food and rich in sacrificial gifts, endowed with every excellence.
t.1.1.86: Through the wise counsel of Vāsudeva and the might of Bhīma and Arjuna, having caused Jarāsaṃdha to be slain, and Caidya too, who was proud of his strength,
t.1.1.87: From all sides tributes came to Duryodhana: gems, gold and jewels, and wealth in cattle, elephants and horses.
t.1.1.88: Then, having seen that prosperous fortune of the Pāṇḍavas thus, a very great rage, born of envy, arose in him.
t.1.1.89: And when he saw the assembly hall, like a celestial palace, so finely built by Maya and presented to the Pāṇḍavas, he was consumed with anguish.
t.1.1.90: And there, as he stumbled about as it were in his confusion, he was laughed at by Bhīma, as though he were a low-born man, before the very eyes of Vāsudeva.
t.1.1.92: Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fond of his sons, gave his consent to the dice game. Hearing that, a great anger arose in Vāsudeva.
t.1.1.91: Though he enjoyed many kinds of pleasures and many kinds of jewels, he was reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra as pale, sallow, and thin.
t.1.1.93: He was not very pleased at heart, yet he approved of the quarrels, and he overlooked the terrible wrongs, the dice game and the rest, even when they had grown great.
t.1.1.95: When the sons of Pāṇḍu were victorious, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having heard the exceedingly unwelcome news and having learned the views of Duryodhana, of Karṇa, and likewise of Śakuni, pondered for a long time and then spoke these words to Saṃjaya.
t.1.1.96: Listen to all that I have to say, Saṃjaya; you ought not to find fault with me. You are learned, wise and intelligent, and esteemed by the wise.
t.1.1.94: Casting aside the counsel of Vidura, Droṇa, Bhīṣma and Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, the warrior class slew one another in that tumultuous war.
t.1.1.97: My mind was not set on war, nor do I take pleasure in the destruction of the Kurus; I make no distinction between my own sons and the sons of Pāṇḍu.
t.1.1.98: My sons, given over to anger, resent me because I am old; but I, blind as I am, bear it out of weakness and love for my sons, and when the senseless Duryodhana is deluded, I am deluded along with him.
t.1.1.100: Resentful, unable by himself to conquer the Pāṇḍavas in battle, and lacking the resolve to win their fortune, like one who is not a kṣatriya, he, together with the king of Gāndhāra, plotted a deceitful game of dice.
t.1.1.99: Having seen the splendor of the mighty Pāṇḍava at the Rājasūya, and having met with that mockery while viewing the assembly hall as he climbed up into it,
t.1.1.101: Hear, Saṃjaya, whatever I came to know in that matter, and how I came to know it. For once you have heard my words, truly joined with reason, you will then know me, O Sauti, to be one whose eye is wisdom.
t.1.1.102: When I heard that the wondrous bow had been drawn, the target pierced and brought down to the earth, and Kṛṣṇā carried off while all the kings looked on, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.103: When I heard that in Dvārakā Subhadrā, the Mādhavī, had been carried off by force by Arjuna, and that the two Vṛṣṇi heroes had gone to Indraprastha, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.105: When I heard that Yudhiṣṭhira, defeated by Saubala at the game of dice, had been robbed of his kingdom, and yet was still followed by his brothers of immeasurable might, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.104: When I heard that the king of the gods, pouring down rain, was held back by Arjuna with divine arrows, and that Agni was thus satisfied in the Khāṇḍava forest, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.106: When I heard that Draupadī, her throat choked with tears, grief-stricken, wearing a single garment and in her menses, had been dragged into the assembly hall as though she had no protectors though she had them, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.107: When I heard, dear Saṃjaya, of the various doings of the Pāṇḍavas, righteous-souled, who had set out for the forest and were suffering out of love for their eldest brother, then I had no hope of victory, Saṃjaya.
t.1.1.108: When I heard that the Dharmarāja, dwelling in the forest, was followed by thousands of snātakas, great-souled brāhmaṇas who live on alms, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.109: When I heard that Arjuna, having satisfied in battle the god of gods, the three-eyed Tryambaka in the form of a Kirāta, obtained that great weapon, the Pāśupata, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.110: When I heard that Dhanaṃjaya, dwelling in the threefold heaven, was duly learning the divine weapon directly from Śakra himself, that praised one, true to his promise, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.111: When I heard that Bhīma and the other Pārthas had met with Vaiśravaṇa in that region inaccessible to men, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.112: When I heard that my own sons, who had gone on the cattle-station expedition and who delighted in Karṇa's counsel, were taken captive by the Gandharvas and set free by Arjuna, then, Saṃjaya, I no longer hoped for victory.
t.1.1.113: When I heard that Dharma, in the form of a Yakṣa, had met with the Dharmarāja, O Sūta, and that he had rightly answered the questions put to him, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.114: When I heard that the foremost of my men had been broken by the great-souled Dhanaṃjaya with a single chariot while he was dwelling in the kingdom of Virāṭa, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.115: When I heard that the king of the Matsyas had honorably given his daughter Uttarā to Arjuna, and that Arjuna had accepted her on behalf of his son, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.116: When I heard that Yudhiṣṭhira, defeated, stripped of wealth, sent into exile and cut off from his own kin, had gathered seven akṣauhiṇīs, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.118: When I heard that Mādhava Vāsudeva, of whom they say that this whole earth was but a single stride, was devoted with his whole self to the cause of the Pāṇḍavas, then, Saṃjaya, I no longer hoped for victory.
t.1.1.117: When I heard Nārada declare that Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and say, “I shall always behold them in the world of Brahmā,” then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.119: When I heard that Karṇa and Duryodhana had made up their minds to seize Keśava, and that he then showed himself in many forms, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.120: When I heard that, as Vāsudeva was departing, Pṛthā stood alone in front of his chariot, distressed, and was consoled by Keśava, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.122: When I heard that Karṇa said to Bhīṣma, "I will not fight while you are fighting," and that, abandoning the army, he went away, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.121: When I heard that Vāsudeva was their counsellor, and likewise that Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, and Bhāradvāja were pronouncing blessings upon them, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.123: When I heard that those two, Vāsudeva and Arjuna, and likewise the immeasurable bow Gāṇḍiva, those three of fierce might, had come together, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.124: When I heard that Arjuna, overcome by despondency, was sinking down on the seat of his chariot, and that Kṛṣṇa showed him the worlds within his own body, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.126: When I heard that Bhīṣma, exceedingly heroic and unassailable in battles, had been slain by Pārtha, who had placed Śikhaṇḍin in front of him, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.125: When I heard that Bhīṣma, the tormentor of foes, was slaying ten thousand chariots in battle, and yet not one of those of conspicuous form among them was slain, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.127: When I heard that the aged hero Bhīṣma, having left the Somakas but few in number, lay upon a bed of arrows, struck down by arrows with bright-colored feathers, then, Saṃjaya, I no longer hoped for victory.
t.1.1.128: When I heard that, as the son of Śaṃtanu lay there wanting water, Arjuna, being asked, split open the earth and quenched Bhīṣma's thirst there, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.130: When I heard that Droṇa, a warrior of brilliant skill in battle, though displaying the various paths of weaponry, could not slay the Pāṇḍavas, the very best of men, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.129: When I heard that Śukra and the Sun stood in conjunction, favourable to the sons of Kuntī for their victory, and that beasts of prey were ceaselessly howling at us, then, Saṃjaya, I no longer hoped for victory.
t.1.1.131: When I heard that our great chariot-warriors, the Saṃśaptakas, who had stood firm to bring about Arjuna's death, were slain by Arjuna, then, Saṃjaya, I no longer hoped for victory.
t.1.1.132: When I heard that the heroic son of Subhadrā, all alone, had broken into and entered the battle array that others could not pierce, guarded by Bhāradvāja with weapons in hand, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.133: When the great chariot-warriors, unable to overcome Pārtha, all surrounded the boy Abhimanyu, slew him, and were filled with delight, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.134: When I heard that the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having slain Abhimanyu, were shouting, bewildered with joy, and that Arjuna had loosed his wrath upon the Saindhava, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.135: When I heard of the vow concerning the Saindhava, the vow made by Arjuna for his slaying, and that he had fulfilled it truly in the midst of his enemies, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.136: When I heard that, Dhanaṃjaya's horses being weary, Vāsudeva unyoked them, watered them, and, when they had been brought back refreshed, yoked them again and drove on, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.137: When I heard that, while the horses were catching their breath, Arjuna, with the Gāṇḍiva resting on the chariot's seat, held back all the warriors, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.138: When I heard that Yuyudhāna, the Vārṣṇeya, having crushed the army of Droṇa, which even forces of elephants could hardly withstand, had gone to where those two, Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha, were, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.139: When I heard that the hero Bhīma, having come up against Karṇa, was spared from death by Karṇa, who reviled him with words and prodded him with the tip of his bow, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.140: When Droṇa, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, Karṇa, Drauṇi and the valiant king of the Madras allowed the Saindhava to be slain, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.141: When I heard that the divine spear given by the king of the gods had been made to miss its mark by Mādhava, spent upon Ghaṭotkaca, the Rākṣasa of fearsome form, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.142: When I heard that in the fight between Karṇa and Ghaṭotkaca the son of the sūta had loosed the spear by which Savyasācin was to be slain in battle, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.144: When I heard that Nakula the Pāṇḍava, son of Mādrī, engaged in single chariot combat with Drauṇi in the midst of the world, was fighting him as an equal in battle, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.143: When I heard that Droṇa, the teacher, alone and seated on the floor of his chariot, having resolved to fast unto death, was cut down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who transgressed dharma, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.145: When, Droṇa having been slain, the son of Droṇa, deploying the divine Nārāyaṇa weapon, did not bring about the end of these Pāṇḍavas, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.146: When I heard that Karṇa, exceedingly heroic and unassailable in battles, had been slain by Pārtha in that strife of brothers, a mystery of the gods, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.147: When I heard that Droṇa's son, Kṛpa, Duḥśāsana and the fierce Kṛtavarman assailed Yudhiṣṭhira when he was left unguarded, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.148: When I heard, O Sūta, that the king of the Madras, that hero who always vies with Kṛṣṇa in battle, had been slain in combat by the Dharmarāja, then, O Saṃjaya, I no longer hoped for victory.
t.1.1.150: When I heard that Duryodhana, weary and alone, chariotless and with his pride broken, had gone to the lake, stilled its waters and lay there, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.149: When I heard that the wicked Saubala, the root of the quarrel and the dice game, whose strength lay in deceit, had been slain in battle by Sahadeva the Pāṇḍava, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.153: When I heard that the Pāñcālas and the sons of Draupadī, while they slept, had been slain by those men led by the son of Droṇa, a loathsome and infamous deed, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.151: When I heard that the Pāṇḍavas, standing with Vāsudeva at the lake of the Gaṅgā, were taunting my unforbearing son, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.154: When I heard that Aśvatthāman, pursued by Bhīmasena and enraged, had launched the supreme weapon, the Aiṣīka, by which he destroyed the embryo, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.152: When I heard, dear one, that he, circling through various maneuvers in the mace fight, had been struck down unfairly through the counsel of Vāsudeva, then, Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.155: When I heard that the Brahmaśiras weapon had been released by Arjuna with the words "May it be well!" and that the weapon had been quelled by his own weapon, and that the jewel, finest of gems, had been given up by Aśvatthāman, then, O Saṃjaya, I had no hope of victory.
t.1.1.157: Gāndhārī is to be pitied, bereft of sons and grandsons, and likewise the daughters-in-law, bereft of fathers and brothers. A deed hard to accomplish has been done by the sons of Pāṇḍu, and the kingdom, free of rivals, has been regained by them.
t.1.1.156: When I heard that, as the great weapon was being hurled by the son of Droṇa into the womb of Vairāṭī, Dvaipāyana and Keśava, one after the other, cursed the son of Droṇa with curses.
t.1.1.158: Alas, I have heard that only ten survived the war, three of ours and seven of the Pāṇḍavas, and that eighteen akṣauhiṇīs were slain in that battle, in that clash of the kṣatriyas.
t.1.1.160: Having spoken thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, deeply grieved, lamented and fainted; then, having recovered again, he addressed these words to Saṃjaya.
t.1.1.159: Overspread with darkness, delusion seems to enter into me; I cannot regain my senses, O Sūta, and my mind seems to reel.
t.1.1.161: Saṃjaya, now that things have come to this, I wish to give up my life without delay, for I see not even the slightest fruit in holding on to life.
t.1.1.162: To that lord of the earth, wretched and lamenting as he spoke thus, the wise Gāvalgaṇi addressed these words of great meaning.
t.1.1.164: Those born in great royal lineages that were endowed with virtues, knowers of divine weapons, whose splendor equaled that of Śakra.
t.1.1.165: Having conquered the earth through dharma, having sacrificed with sacrifices accompanied by ample gifts, and having attained fame in this world, they then passed under the sway of Time.
t.1.1.166: Vainya, the great chariot-warrior and hero; Sṛñjaya, best of victors; Suhotra and Rantideva; and likewise Kakṣīvant, son of Uśij.
t.1.1.163: You have indeed heard, from Dvaipāyana as he spoke and from the wise Nārada, of the king's great zeal and great might.
t.1.1.167: Vāhlīka, Damana, Śaibya, and Śaryāti, unconquered yet conquered; Viśvāmitra, slayer of foes, and Ambarīṣa of great strength.
t.1.1.168: Marutta, Manu, Ikṣvāku, Gaya, and Bharata as well, and also Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, Śaśabindu, and Bhagīratha;
t.1.1.170: Thus were these twenty-four kings recounted long ago by Nārada, the divine seer, to Śaibya, who was burning with grief for his son.
t.1.1.169: Yayāti of auspicious deeds, who was made to offer sacrifice by the gods themselves, and whose earth here, marked with shrines and sacrificial posts, was a mine of soma-pressings.
t.1.1.171: And other kings, mightier even than these, have passed away before: great chariot-warriors, great-souled men endowed with every virtue.
t.1.1.172: Pūru, Kuru, Yadu, Śūra, Viṣvagaśva of great fortitude, the sinless Yuvanāśva, Kakutstha, and the valiant Raghu,
t.1.1.173: The victorious Vītihotra, and Bhava, Śveta, Bṛhadguru, Uśīnara, Śataratha, Kaṅka, Duliduha and Druma.
t.1.1.174: Dambhodbhava, the eminent Vena, Sagara, Saṃkṛti, Nimi, the invincible Paraśu, Puṇḍra, Śambhu, and the sinless Devāvṛdha.
t.1.1.175: Devāhvaya, Supratima, Supratīka, Bṛhadratha, Sukratu, and Nala the Naiṣadha, a man of great energy and disciplined self.
t.1.1.176: Satyavrata, Śāntabhaya, Sumitra, the mighty lord Subala, Jānujaṅgha, Anaraṇya, Arka, Priyabhṛtya, and Śubhavrata.
t.1.1.177: Balabandhu, Nirāmarda, Ketuśṛṅga, Bṛhadbala, Dhṛṣṭaketu, Bṛhatketu, Dīptaketu, and Nirāmaya.
t.1.1.179: These and many others are heard of, by hundreds and by thousands, and still others by tens of thousands, and they have even been counted by the padma.
t.1.1.178: Avikṣit, Prabala, Dhūrta, Kṛtabandhu, Dṛḍheṣudhi, the great and ancient Saṃbhāvya, Pratyaṅga the slayer of foes, and Śruti.
t.1.1.180: Leaving behind their abundant riches and pleasures, wise and mighty kings, the very greatest, have met their death through your sons.
t.1.1.182: It is told in the world by learned men, by the ancient and most excellent poets, that even those who were endowed with every prosperity and virtue have gone to their death.
t.1.1.183: Your sons were evil-minded, consumed by wrath, greedy, and for the most part wicked in conduct; you ought not to grieve for them.
t.1.1.184: You are learned, wise, intelligent, and esteemed by the wise. Those whose understanding follows the śāstras are not bewildered, Bhārata.
t.1.1.186: That was bound to happen thus, and therefore you should not grieve. Who, by any excellence of wisdom, can turn back fate?
t.1.1.185: Both restraint and indulgence are known to you, O lord of men; boundless compliance is not taught in the protection of a son.
t.1.1.181: Those whose deeds were divine, whose were valor and generosity as well, greatness of spirit too, and faith, truthfulness, purity, and uprightness.
t.1.1.187: No one transgresses the path ordained by the Ordainer. All this has Time as its root: being and non-being, happiness and unhappiness.
t.1.1.188: Time ripens all beings, and Time destroys all creatures; and when Time is consuming the creatures, it is Time again that brings it to rest.
t.1.1.189: Time transforms all states of being in the world, the auspicious and the inauspicious. Time draws in all creatures and sends them forth again. Time moves among all beings, unrestrained and impartial.
t.1.1.190: The things that are past and yet to come, and those that exist at present, know them all to be fashioned by Time, and you should not lose your senses.
t.1.1.191: Here Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke a holy upaniṣad: through the meritorious study of the Bhārata, all the sins of one who has faith and recites even a single quarter-verse are purified without remainder.
t.1.1.192: For here are celebrated the holy divine seers, and likewise the Brahmin seers and royal seers of auspicious deeds, as well as the Yakṣas and the great serpents.
t.1.1.193: And here the eternal Lord Vāsudeva is glorified, for he is truth and cosmic order, the purifier and the holy.
t.1.1.194: He is the eternal, supreme Brahman, the steadfast, everlasting light, whose divine deeds the wise recount.
t.1.1.195: From that god proceed the unreal and the real, the real and the unreal, and from him too come continuity and activity, birth, death, and rebirth.
t.1.1.196: That which is taught as the inner self, made up of the qualities of the five elements, and that which is supreme, beginning with the unmanifest: he alone is the one celebrated in song.
t.1.1.198: A man who is full of faith, ever diligent, and devoted to truth and dharma, and who earnestly studies this chapter, is freed from sin.
t.1.1.197: That which the foremost of ascetics, disciplined and endowed with the power of meditation and yoga, behold abiding within the self, like a reflection in a mirror.
t.1.1.199: The believer who constantly listens to this chapter of the Bhārata, the Anukramaṇī, from the beginning, does not sink down in difficulties.
t.1.1.200: One who recites even a little of the Anukramaṇī at both twilights is at once freed from whatever sin he may have accumulated during the day and the night.
t.1.1.201: For this is the very body of the Bhārata, its truth and its nectar of immortality, like fresh butter drawn from curd, like the brāhmaṇa among two-footed beings.
t.1.1.202: Of all bodies of water the ocean is the best, and of four-footed creatures the cow is the most excellent; just as these are the most excellent, so is the Bhārata said to be.
t.1.1.203: Whoever has the brahmins listen to even a quarter of this at a śrāddha, the food and drink he offers reaches his ancestors and becomes imperishable.
t.1.1.204: One should amplify the Veda by means of the Itihāsa and the Purāṇa. The Veda is afraid of one of little learning, thinking, "This one will mislead me."
t.1.1.205: The wise man who causes others to hear this Veda of Kṛṣṇa obtains his aim, and he would cast off even the sin committed by killing an embryo; of this there is no doubt.
t.1.1.206: Whoever, being pure, recites this chapter at every parvan, by him the entire Bhārata would have been studied; such is my opinion.
t.1.1.207: And the man who constantly listens with faith to this work of the seer would obtain long life, fame, and the attainment of heaven.
t.1.1.208: Long ago the assembled gods and seers placed on a scale the four Vedas on one side and the Bhārata alone on the other; and when it was weighed, it proved greater than they in both magnitude and weight.
t.1.1.209: Because of its greatness and its weightiness, it is called the Mahābhārata. Whoever knows the explanation of this name is freed from all sins.
t.1.1.210: Austerity is no sin, study is no sin, the Vedic ordinance that accords with one's own nature is no sin, and even seizing wealth by force is no sin; it is these very things, when corrupted by wrongful intent, that become sin.
